title: Diceware and the Combinatorics of a Memorable Passphrase
explainer: The lesson's "four random words beats a short complex-looking password" claim is a direct application of basic combinatorics: a passphrase's resistance to guessing comes from how many possibilities an attacker must search, not how exotic it looks. That count is measured in bits of entropy — roughly the log base 2 of the number of equally likely passphrases a given scheme can produce — a method formalized by Arnold Reinhold's 1995 "Diceware" word list, which maps rolls of five dice to one of 7,776 words so anyone can generate a passphrase with a precisely countable amount of randomness. A handful of ordinary words from a large list beats a short string of symbols because multiplying thousands of choices together several times over outgrows a small character set raised to a much smaller exponent.

title: Where 'Phishing' Comes From
explainer: "Phishing" is spelled with "ph" on purpose — it borrows the convention from 1970s "phone phreaking," the subculture that hacked analog telephone networks (famously using tones to trick switching equipment into granting free long-distance calls) to explore and exploit the phone system for free. By the mid-1990s the same "ph" spelling resurfaced among people trying to steal America Online accounts by posing as AOL staff and asking users to "verify" their password — the exact credential-harvesting pattern the lesson's sample email still follows decades later, just moved from instant messages to email and lookalike login pages.
